'''Mary Ellen Rickett''' (4 March 1861 – 20 March 1925) was a British mathematician who lectured in mathematics at [[Newnham College, Cambridge|Newnham College, University of Cambridge]] for more than twenty years. She was also the Vice-Principal of Old Hall from 1895 until her death in 1925. She was the first woman to win [[Bedford College, London|Bedford College]]'s Gold Medal when she graduated with her bachelor's degree, and the first [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|Wrangler]] of Newnham College.

== Life ==
Rickett was born on 4 March 1861.<ref name="Haines2001">{{cite book |last=Haines |first=Catharine M. C. |url=https://archive.org/details/internationalwom00hain |title=International Women in Science: A Biographical Dictionary to 1950 |publisher=ABC-CLIO |year=2001 |isbn=978-1-57607-090-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/internationalwom00hain/page/262 262] |chapter=Bromhall, Margaret Ann |url-access=registration}}</ref> She was educated by private tutors, and then at a private school in [[Brighton]], and at Priory School in [[Dover]].<ref name="camrev">{{citation|title=News of the Week and Notes|page=110|journal=The Cambridge Review|date=November 28, 1895|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZAE-AQAAMAAJ&pg=PA110}}</ref><ref name="Haines2001" /> Rickett earned a bachelor's degree in French and German from Bedford College, London, part of the [[University of London]], in 1881, and was the first woman to win the gold medal of the University of London.<ref name="ency">{{citation|url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/women/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/rickett-mary-ellen-1861-1925|contribution=Rickett, Mary Ellen (1861–1925)|via=Encyclopedia.com|title=Dictionary of Women Worldwide: 25,000 Women Through the Ages|publisher=Cengage|access-date=2021-10-23}}</ref>

She studied at Newnham College beginning in 1882, and took both the [[Classical Tripos]] in 1884 and the [[Mathematical Tripos]] in 1885 and 1886.<ref name="camrev" /> In the Mathematical Tripos, her score was next after the 24th Wrangler (and before the 25th Wrangler), making her the first Wrangler of Newnham.<ref name="camrev" /><ref name="creese">{{citation |last=Creese |first=Mary R. S. |title=British women of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries who contributed to research in the chemical sciences |date=September 1991 |journal=The British Journal for the History of Science |volume=24 |issue=3 |pages=275–305 |doi=10.1017/S0007087400027370 |jstor=4027231 |pmid=11622943 |s2cid=27890390 |doi-access=free}}; see footnote 85, p. 299</ref> In 1893, she was elected one of the first thirty associates of the college.<ref name="camrev" />

She became a lecturer in mathematics at Newnham College in 1886,<ref name="camrev" /><ref name="ency" /> associate of the college in 1893,<ref name="camrev" /> acting vice-principal of Old Hall in 1889,<ref name="ency" /> and permanent vice-principal in 1895.<ref name="camrev" /> Rickett was regarded as an "especially successful teacher",<ref name="camrev" /> whose approach was "precise and clear".<ref name="Haines2001" /> In Newnham, she coached [[Philippa Fawcett]] to become the first woman to get the highest score on the Mathematical Tripos, 1890.<ref name="fawcett">{{citation |last=Wooldridge |first=Adrian |title=The Aristocracy of Talent: How Meritocracy Made the Modern World |page=324 |year=2021 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uOU3EAAAQBAJ&pg=PT324 |publisher=Simon and Schuster |isbn=9781510768628}}</ref> Rickett retired in 1908, and died on 20 March 1925, aged 64.<ref name="ency" /><ref name="Haines2001" />
